cf.title: Reset unlogged relations before syncing the data directory?

input.subject: Reset unlogged relations before syncing the data directory?

verdict_reasoning: The goal is clear and the cost falls on nobody who does not benefit, so levels 1a and 1b pass. One fixable level 2 objection survived, replication-ondisk-1: SyncDataDirectory() now runs after InitWalRecovery(), and the thread has no answer on why that is safe. The author asks this in message #1 and no committer has replied. A committer who knows the startup code has to confirm the ordering.

brief.title: Reset unlogged relations before syncing the data directory at crash start
brief.problem: At crash startup, SyncDataDirectory() fsyncs unlogged relation forks that the startup process then removes. That writeback is wasted work and slows crash restart for clusters with large unlogged tables.
brief.proposed_design: On crash starts, the patch runs the unlogged relation cleanup after InitWalRecovery() has restored tablespace links and before SyncDataDirectory(). Init forks and surviving files are still synced before replay, and the end-of-recovery checkpoint does not move. Recovery after a clean shutdown keeps the later cleanup, which runs after pg_control records recovery.
author_claims: With a 1.14 GiB unlogged table, crash startup dropped from a 26.34 s median to 0.40 s with recovery_init_sync_method=fsync.
With recovery_init_sync_method=syncfs, the median dropped from 22.58 s to 0.30 s, because syncfs cannot skip individual files.
The author says the gains may come from dirty data left in the OS page cache after pg_ctl stop -m immediate.
Keeping the late cleanup after a clean shutdown stops a failed start from deleting unlogged files while pg_control still allows a restart without recovery.
brief.thread_state: Chao Li agreed with the change, asked for an explicit InRecovery check, and gave v2 an LGTM. No committer has replied, and the author asked whether the initial sync must happen before InitWalRecovery().
unclear: The proposal does not say what happens if the server crashes again after the early cleanup but before SyncDataDirectory() finishes.
The benchmark has no run with the OS page cache flushed, so the gain under typical crash conditions is unknown.
The material does not say whether a test covers the new ordering, for example a TAP test with unlogged tables in a tablespace.
The proposal does not say whether removing files before the directory sync leaves the unlink itself durable before WAL replay starts.

prior_attempts.title: speed up pg_rewind by using copy_file_range() and skipping some fsync
prior_attempts.quote: Anyway, I think that it would be good to do more benchmarking for this patch first, and the patch you are proposing is enough for that.
prior_attempts.reason: Michael Paquier asked for pg_rewind benchmarks: many small files for the fsync patch, and large and small file sets on XFS with reflink for copy_file_range(). He also asked to drop the copy_file_range_support flag, because one EXDEV failure would turn copy_file_range() off for all other tablespaces and mount points, and to fix double-counted progress on fallback. The fsync patch skips files such as configuration files included from postgresql.conf. The visible messages do not show a reply after his last review.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 skipped fsync of unchanged files in pg_rewind, a different tool and code path. This patch reorders unlogged cleanup and SyncDataDirectory() at crash startup. P4's request for more benchmarks is relevant because message #1 measured only without a cache flush.

objections.title: InitWalRecovery() now runs before the data directory is synced
objections.failure_scenario: The server crashes and restarts. InitWalRecovery() reads the checkpoint record and backup_label from the OS page cache, restores tablespace links and durably renames tablespace_map. Power is lost before SyncDataDirectory() finishes, so the next start finds the renamed map but may not find links or WAL that were never flushed.
objections.argument: The cleanup can only run after the tablespace links exist, so the patch has to move SyncDataDirectory() after InitWalRecovery(). Today the sync runs first, so recovery setup only reads state that is already durable. The proposal does not list which reads and durable renames in InitWalRecovery() would now depend on unsynced files. In message #1 the author asks this same question, and no committer has answered it in messages #2-#4.
objections.author_must_show: Which files does InitWalRecovery() read or rename on a crash start, and why is each step safe if the OS loses unsynced data before SyncDataDirectory() completes?

critic.reasoning: The sync does move after InitWalRecovery(), and message #1 asks whether that is safe without getting an answer. The stated scenario is weaker than written, because tablespace links are created after the sync today too, but the question about reads of unsynced files stands.

refuted.title: Split cleanup ordering relies on untested startup invariants
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch reorders StartupXLOG, for example moving SyncDataDirectory() or the early cleanup ahead of InitWalRecovery(). The cleanup then runs before tablespace links from tablespace_map exist, so unlogged forks in those tablespaces survive a crash with stale contents. Users find out only when an unlogged table returns old rows after restart.
refuted.argument: The patch makes ResetUnloggedRelations() run at two different points, chosen by start type, and each point depends on its own ordering reason (tablespace links before it, pg_control state after it). Message #2 shows that the gating also depends on an implicit rule, didCrash implies InRecovery, now covered by a redundant check. Only xlog.c is touched, so no TAP test fails if a future reordering breaks either rule. The author's own question in message #1 about moving the sync shows this ordering is still open to change.
refuted.author_must_show: Which test would fail if a later patch moved the early cleanup before InitWalRecovery(), for example a crash start with unlogged tables in a tablespace?

critic.reasoning: The failure needs a later patch that reorders StartupXLOG against a reason the commit message already states, and v2 adds the explicit InRecovery check. The request for a TAP test is level 4, which is out of scope here.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The patch changes when unlogged relation files are removed relative to the crash-start data directory sync; no format change.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch reorders InitWalRecovery(), unlogged cleanup and SyncDataDirectory() in the startup process in xlog.c.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The unlogged cleanup now runs at two points chosen by start type, each with its own ordering reason.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which files does InitWalRecovery() read or rename on a crash start, and why is each step safe if the OS loses unsynced data before SyncDataDirectory() completes?
What happens if the server crashes or loses power after the early cleanup but before SyncDataDirectory() finishes?
What are the patched and unpatched crash startup times when the OS page cache is flushed before restart?
Does a test cover a crash start with unlogged tables in a tablespace under the new ordering?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows StartupXLOG, InitWalRecovery() and the crash-start fsync rules has to sign off; no committer has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for crash-start durability under the new ordering, including a second crash before the sync finishes, for as long as the ordering stands.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 three days after the review in message #2 and asked an open design question, which suggests continued engagement.

priority.reason: The patch is about 4 KiB in one file and helps clusters with large unlogged tables on crash restart, with no user-visible surface. It waits on a committer who knows the startup code to answer the ordering question from message #1.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the exact position of SyncDataDirectory() relative to the steps inside InitWalRecovery() could not be checked. Message #4 was not shown.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unlogged relation copy is not fsync'd
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes the condition in RelationCopyStorage() so that the main and other non-init forks of an unlogged relation are fsync'd after copying, for example during alter table ... set tablespace. Without the fix, a checkpoint during the copy followed by a clean shutdown and power loss can lose part of the copied file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that the posted patch was still incomplete and proposed a broader backpatchable fix that calls smgrimmedsync() for all but temporary relations, with similar changes in nbtsort.c, gistbuild.c and rewriteheap.c. Noah Misch questioned part of that analysis, and no revised patch followed. After about three months with no new version, Robert Haas marked the entry Returned with feedback as waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So it seems this has been waiting for
Heikki or someone else to have time to work it for the last 3 months.

precedents_retrieved.title: Startup Centralization
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set routes all postmaster child forks, including autovacuum, syslogger, archiver, bgworkers and backends, through StartChildProcess, using a ForkProcData struct that describes each process type. The process type is then set before InitPostmasterChild, so a new early-startup hook (InitPostmasterChild_hook) can see which kind of process is starting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund said the patch was far from ready and might be going in the wrong direction. He asked that each process type's properties be defined in one array of structs, and that the EXEC_BACKEND code be centralized too. He also listed concrete defects: a memory leak in postmaster_forkexec, more reliance on global variables, and process-type messages that were no longer translatable. He was not convinced the hook was useful. The author agreed to rework the patch but sent no new version, so Michael Paquier closed the entry as returned with feedback because the comments were not addressed and the patch no longer applied to HEAD.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: In short, I think this is far from ready, nor am I sure this is going in the right direction.

precedents_retrieved.title: Detectable crashes and unlogged table resets
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread started with a per-table flag in the init fork so applications could detect that an unlogged table was reset after a crash, mainly for sharded setups where one shard can be lost. It moved to a server-wide record in pg_control of the last crash recovery (LSN, time and a counter), read through a SQL function, with an attached patch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Discussion stopped after June 2021 with open questions: whether LSN or timestamp is useful (Tom Lane doubted LSN), whether to reset the counter, and whether to track promotions. The entry moved through four commitfests with no further activity, and Michael Paquier closed it because it had been idle too long.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This is too long, so let's discard this patch for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: speed up pg_rewind by using copy_file_range() and skipping some fsync
precedents_retrieved.summary: Two pg_rewind patches: one syncs only the files pg_rewind changed instead of the whole target data directory, and one uses copy_file_range() in place of read()+write() for local rewinds. The second adds a configure check and HAVE_COPY_FILE_RANGE and falls back to read()+write() on EXDEV or ENOTSUP.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier asked for pg_rewind benchmarks: many small files for the fsync patch, and large and small file sets on XFS with reflink for copy_file_range(). He also asked to drop the copy_file_range_support flag, because one EXDEV failure would turn copy_file_range() off for all other tablespaces and mount points, and to fix double-counted progress on fallback. The fsync patch skips files such as configuration files included from postgresql.conf. The visible messages do not show a reply after his last review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Anyway, I think that it would be good to do more benchmarking for this
patch first, and the patch you are proposing is enough for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fsync queue forgets requests on failure
precedents_retrieved.summary: Fix the checkpointer so that when an fsync of a relation segment fails during a checkpoint, the pending fsync request is kept for the next checkpoint instead of being dropped. The patch stops the pending-ops bitmapset from being lost when it is unlinked from the hashtable entry, merges unprocessed requests back on failure, and removes segments that succeeded as it goes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as redundant with work in another thread (by Craig and Andres) that turns fsync I/O errors into PANICs and overhauls the request queue, because retrying fsync after a failure is useless on Linux. He noted that the other patch still left the retry path for errnos other than EIO and ENOSPC, but rejected this entry on the grounds that the issue would be resolved in that other thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Rejected, since this will have to be dealt with one way or another in
that other thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Startup Centralization
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set routes all postmaster children (auxiliary processes, autovacuum launcher and workers, syslogger, archiver, bgworkers) through one fork and startup path, so the process type is set right after fork. It adds a subprocess array describing each process type and a hook in early child startup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not post the promised revision for two months, so Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback. The revision was to make the process_types array stop depending on the order of the enum in subprocess.h, add the subprocess pids array, and rebase after the 0009 patch stopped applying. Peter Eisentraut also objected to renaming AuxProcType to SubprocessType and the related files.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Nothing has happened here in two months, so I am marking this stuff as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generalize ereport_startup_progress infrastructure
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the ereport_startup_progress infrastructure into elog.c/.h as a generic ereport_progress API, renames log_startup_progress_interval to log_progress_report_interval, and passes the interval to begin_progress_report_phase(). Follow-up patches would use it for postmaster removal of temp files and temp relation files, and later for checkpointer file processing.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said neither proposed use was the right way to solve its problem. The postmaster use changed timeout.c and relied on the timeout infrastructure, which he did not consider safe there. The checkpointer use needed more design work on how it interacts with log_checkpoints and the existing checkpoint logging. The author withdrew the entry about two weeks after his last message, which proposed new GUC designs and got no visible reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: At the same time, I don't think the overall picture here is too clear yet. I'm reluctant to commit to a specific UI for a feature whose scope we don't seem to know.

precedents_retrieved.title: reduce impact of lengthy startup and checkpoint tasks
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds a new auxiliary process, the custodian, that takes slow O(n) cleanup work out of startup and checkpoints. Later versions move removal of old serialized logical decoding snapshots and logical rewrite mapping files to it, with temporary file cleanup planned for a follow-up thread.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected again to moving snapshot and mapping file removal to the custodian, because without further work this raises the wraparound risk tied to the file names. Tom Lane said there was little point in going ahead without the RemovePgTempFiles task, which had been dropped from the patch set, and asked whether a long-lived custodian is the right model at all. The author planned a reworked version for the July commitfest but had none ready when asked.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Hmm, given Andres' objections there's little point in moving forward without that task.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
Reverted commit(s): Remove some unstable parts from new TAP test for archive status check
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This part of the test was included originally in 4e87c48, but got
reverted as of f9c1b8d because of timing issues in the test, where,
after more analysis, we found that the standbys may not have recovered
from the archives all the segments needed by the test.  This stabilizes
the test by making sure that standbys replay up to the position returned
by pg_switch_wal(), meaning that all segments are recovered before the
manual checkpoint that tests WAL segment recycling and its interactions
with archive status files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
Reverted commit(s): Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process.; Fix segmentation fault that commit ac22929a26 caused.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert ac22929a26, as well as the followup fix 113d3591b8. Because it broke
the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict
on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled
in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(). It caused, for example,
SIGHUP signal handler or walreceiver process to wake that startup process
up unnecessarily frequently.

Additionally, add the comments about why that dedicated latch that
the reverted patch tried to get rid of should not be removed.

Thanks to Kyotaro Horiguchi for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent tried this reordering, and P10's reason, about a custodian process and file-name wraparound, does not apply. P4 asked for benchmarks, but here that is a performance-evidence question for the other angles, not a prior rejection reason. The thread points to no earlier discussion of the same idea.

The patch changes only the order of startup steps in xlog.c, with no new syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql change or dump content. Unlogged tables are already emptied after a crash, so users and clients see the same result. Crash-safety of the new ordering belongs to another angle.

The patch changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, protocol or ABI. Unlinks done before the sync become durable once SyncDataDirectory() fsyncs the directories. A crash during the early cleanup leads to another crash start, which runs the cleanup again.

The patch only reorders crash-startup steps inside the startup process, which runs before any client can connect. It adds no SQL surface, GUC, privilege, role or monitoring output, so no user can reach it or learn anything new. Its durability and crash-ordering questions belong to the safety angle.

The change is small, confined to crash startup, and adds no per-query, per-tuple or per-backend cost, no new GUC and no external dependency. No committer has engaged yet, which affects committability, not the merits.

No existing feature does this job. Both values of recovery_init_sync_method, fsync and syncfs, still write back the unlogged forks, and fsync = off gives up durability for every file. No extension or hook can change the order of steps inside the startup process, so the change has to be in core. The patch reorders existing calls and adds no second mechanism. Not checked: whether the reorder is safe and whether the gain holds with a cold page cache; other angles cover these.

No demand objection stands. The patch adds no GUC, syntax or catalog change and touches only xlog.c, so users who do not benefit pay almost nothing. The gain applies whenever the postmaster does a crash restart without an OS reboot, which is the default restart_after_crash case where dirty unlogged pages remain in the page cache. The thread has no field report, and the benchmark covers only the dirty-cache case, but a benefit-only internal change does not need broad demand evidence.
